n: A short parable begins. Israel was often pictured as a vine God planted; here the image takes an unexpected turn.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

n: What makes a vine’s wood better than any forest tree? Grapevines are valuable only for their fruit; their wood is twisted and weak.
You can’t build anything from vine wood—not even a peg to hang a pot on.
It’s only good for fuel. And after the fire chars both ends and the middle, it’s good for even less. Judah had been “burned” already by earlier Babylonian invasions.

f.w: the fire devoureth both the ends of it
f.g: Perhaps Judah’s earlier losses in 605 and 597 BC.

n: If it was useless when whole, how much more after it has been burned! A vine that bears no fruit has no other purpose.

f.w: when it was whole, it was meet for no work

n: So it is with Jerusalem: a fruitless vine fit only for burning. Its value depended on producing the fruit of righteousness.

f.w: so will I give the inhabitants of Jerusalem

n: Some have escaped one fire, but another will catch them. Survivors of earlier invasions will not escape the final one.

f.w: they shall go out from one fire, and another fire shall devour them

n: The land will be made desolate because they were unfaithful.

f.g: Hebrew ma‘al—unfaithfulness, a breach of trust against God.
